topics.name: The Tudors: Edward, Mary and Elizabeth to 1603
Russia: Alexander II to Nicholas II, 1855-1917

cards: Evaluate how convincing three extracts are in relation to the question, using own knowledge to support and challenge each one. No overall comparison is required.
Evaluate the value of three sources for an enquiry, considering provenance (author, audience, purpose), tone and emphasis, and content with own knowledge.
Argue a clear judgement, balance factors, use precise evidence, and link back to the question in every paragraph.
A 3,000-4,500 word independent investigation covering a period of about 100 years, using primary sources and historians' interpretations.
Identify each extract's overall argument, then test its claims against precise own knowledge, saying how far it is convincing.
Consider who wrote it, when, why and for whom; explain how these affect the source's value, not just that they do.
Reach a substantiated conclusion that weighs factors, explaining why one is more significant than others.
Henry VII's claim to the throne
Weak: through his mother, Margaret Beaufort, descended from John of Gaunt's legitimised Beaufort line. Won at Bosworth (1485) against Richard III.
Dated his reign from the day before Bosworth, married Elizabeth of York (1486), and dealt with pretenders: Lambert Simnel (Stoke, 1487) and Perkin Warbeck (executed 1499).
Used bonds and recognisances, Acts of Attainder and the Council Learned in the Law to control the nobles; limited retaining.
Increased income from crown lands, customs duties and feudal dues; left a healthy treasury. Empson and Dudley were unpopular agents.
Sought security and recognition: Treaty of Medina del Campo (1489) with Spain, Treaty of Étaples (1492) with France, and the marriage of Margaret to James IV of Scotland (1503).
Rising against taxation for war with Scotland; defeated at Blackheath.
Henry Tudor defeated Richard III, helped by the Stanleys' intervention and French-backed troops.
Relied on loyal advisers such as Morton, Fox, Bray and Lovell; the Great Council met only occasionally.
Henry VII increased their duties in local government and law and order, reducing reliance on great nobles.
Rising against taxation for war in Brittany; the Earl of Northumberland was killed.
Margaret of Burgundy backed Simnel and Warbeck; Henry imposed a trade embargo (1493-96) until the Magnus Intercursus (1496).
Marriage of Arthur and Catherine of Aragon
1501, sealing the Spanish alliance; Arthur died in 1502, and Catherine was later betrothed to Prince Henry.
After 1502, increasing use of bonds and financial pressure made the regime seem harsher and more insecure.
Lord Chancellor and cardinal; dominated government 1515-29; Field of the Cloth of Gold (1520) and Treaty of London (1518); fell after failing to secure the annulment.
Henry sought an annulment from Catherine of Aragon, citing Leviticus, as he lacked a male heir and wanted to marry Anne Boleyn.
Act in Restraint of Appeals (1533) and Act of Supremacy (1534) made Henry Supreme Head of the Church of England.
Chief minister 1532-40; organised the break with Rome and the dissolution of the monasteries; Elton argued for a 'Tudor revolution in government'. Executed after the Anne of Cleves marriage.
Smaller monasteries closed in 1536 and larger ones by 1540, transferring wealth to the crown.
The largest Tudor rebellion, in the north, led by Robert Aske; motivated by religion, economics and politics. Henry promised concessions, then executed leaders.
Wars with France and Scotland in the 1540s; capture of Boulogne (1544) at great cost; debasement of the coinage.
Arrested Empson and Dudley to win popularity, and married Catherine of Aragon.
War with France (1512-14) brought the Battle of the Spurs and capture of Tournai and Thérouanne; Flodden (1513) defeated the Scots.
Wolsey's non-parliamentary tax for war with France provoked resistance and was abandoned.
Papal legate from 1518; criticised for pluralism, absenteeism and wealth, though he planned some reforms.
Married Henry in 1533; mother of Elizabeth; executed in 1536 after factional plotting.
Henry married Jane in 1536; she gave birth to Edward in 1537 and died soon after.
Ten Articles (1536) leaned Protestant; the Act of Six Articles (1539) reaffirmed Catholic doctrine.
Rivalry between conservatives (Norfolk, Gardiner) and reformers (Cromwell, Cranmer, the Seymours) shaped policy.
Historians debate whether 1547-58 was a crisis: rebellions, religious change and economic problems vs continuity of government.
Somerset then Northumberland ruled as regents. Protestant reforms: Book of Common Prayer (1549 and 1552). 1549 Western and Kett's rebellions.
Restored Catholicism, married Philip of Spain (Wyatt's rebellion 1554), burned around 280 Protestants and lost Calais (1558).
Acts of Supremacy and Uniformity created a moderate Protestant church; Elizabeth was Supreme Governor.
Northern Rebellion 1569, papal bull of excommunication 1570, Ridolfi, Throckmorton and Babington plots; Mary, Queen of Scots executed 1587.
Vestments controversy, prophesyings (Archbishop Grindal), presbyterian movement and the Marprelate tracts.
Defeated by English fireships at Gravelines and bad weather; boosted Elizabeth's prestige but war with Spain continued.
Factional rivalry (Essex vs Cecil), Essex rebellion (1601), war in Ireland, poor harvests, inflation and the Poor Law of 1601.
Blamed for rebellions, the costly war with Scotland and inflation; overthrown by Northumberland.
Norfolk rising over enclosure and economic grievances, camped at Mousehold Heath; crushed by Warwick.
Devon and Cornwall rising against the new English Prayer Book.
Northumberland tried to place her on the throne; Mary rallied support and became queen within days.
Suitors included Philip II, Archduke Charles and Anjou; she never married, protecting her independence.
Elizabeth's chief minister and Secretary of State, later Lord Treasurer; a key source of stability.
Elizabeth's spymaster; uncovered the Babington Plot that led to Mary, Queen of Scots' execution.
Parliaments raised money and passed laws; clashes over marriage, succession, religion and monopolies (1601).
Emancipation of the serfs (1861), zemstva (local councils, 1864), judicial reform, military reform and relaxed censorship. Assassinated in 1881.
Repression under Pobedonostsev, Russification, land captains (1889) and economic modernisation under Witte.
Industrialisation in the 1890s: foreign investment, the Trans-Siberian Railway and the gold standard.
Caused by defeat in the Russo-Japanese War and Bloody Sunday. Nicholas issued the October Manifesto, creating the Duma.
Prime Minister 1906-11: repression ('Stolypin's necktie') and agricultural reform (the 'wager on the strong'). Assassinated 1911.
Four Dumas 1906-17; Nicholas used the Fundamental Laws to limit their power and dissolved the first two.
Liberals (Kadets, Octobrists), Socialist Revolutionaries, and Social Democrats split into Bolsheviks (Lenin) and Mensheviks (1903).
War failures, food shortages, strikes in Petrograd and army mutiny led to Nicholas II's abdication; the Provisional Government and Petrograd Soviet shared power (dual power).
Defeat exposed Russia's backwardness and pushed Alexander II towards reform.
Peasants paid redemption payments for 49 years and remained tied to the mir; many received poor land.
1870s 'going to the people' failed; the terrorist group People's Will assassinated Alexander II.
Imposing Russian language and Orthodoxy on minorities such as Poles and Finns; pogroms against Jews.
Troops fired on peaceful marchers led by Father Gapon in St Petersburg, destroying faith in the 'Little Father'.
A peasant mystic who influenced the royal family through Tsarevich Alexei's haemophilia; murdered in December 1916.
Russia in the First World War
Heavy defeats (Tannenberg 1914), Nicholas took personal command (1915), inflation and transport breakdown.
Troops shot striking miners, sparking a wave of strikes before the war.
Bolsheviks seized power in Petrograd, led by Lenin and organised by Trotsky through the Military Revolutionary Committee.
Dissolved the Constituent Assembly (January 1918), signed Brest-Litovsk with Germany (March 1918) and set up the Cheka.
The Reds defeated the Whites thanks to Trotsky's Red Army, central position, unity and the Whites' divisions.
War Communism: grain requisitioning and nationalisation. Kronstadt mutiny (1921) led to the New Economic Policy, allowing private trade.
Created a one-party state with terror; his Testament criticised Stalin. Died January 1924.
'Peace, Land and Bread' and 'All power to the Soviets'; rejected cooperation with the Provisional Government.
Failed uprising in Petrograd; Lenin fled to Finland and the Bolsheviks were blamed.
Attempted military coup in August 1917; Kerensky armed the Bolsheviks, boosting their support.
From 1918 the Cheka arrested and executed opponents; the Tsar's family was killed at Ekaterinburg (July 1918).
At the Tenth Party Congress, Lenin banned factions, centralising control in the party.
Russia lost about a third of its population, much farmland and industry, including Ukraine and the Baltic.
Used his position as General Secretary, the Lenin enrolment, and played off the left (Trotsky, Zinoviev, Kamenev) and right (Bukharin).
Forced merging of farms from 1929; liquidation of the kulaks; famine in Ukraine (1932-33) killed millions.
Rapid heavy industrialisation from 1928; Magnitogorsk; Stakhanovite movement; growth in coal, steel and oil but poor consumer goods.
Purges of the party, army and population 1936-38; show trials; the NKVD under Yezhov; millions sent to gulags.
Operation Barbarossa (1941); victory at Stalingrad (1942-43) and Kursk (1943); around 27 million Soviet deaths.
Secret Speech (1956) denounced Stalin; de-Stalinisation; Virgin Lands scheme; Cuban Missile Crisis (1962). Removed in 1964.
Stalin's policy of building socialism in the USSR first, against Trotsky's Permanent Revolution.
Used as a pretext for the purges; Stalin may have been involved.
Zinoviev and Kamenev (1936), Pyatakov (1937) and Bukharin (1938) confessed to invented crimes.
Tukhachevsky and many senior officers executed in 1937, weakening the army before the war.
Stalin presented as the father of the nation; propaganda, rewritten history and socialist realism.
Zhdanovshchina cultural repression, the Leningrad Affair and the Doctors' Plot (1953). Stalin died in March 1953.
Defeated Beria (executed 1953) and the Anti-Party Group (Malenkov, Molotov) in 1957.
Crushed by Soviet tanks, showing the limits of de-Stalinisation.
Proportional representation, a strong president with Article 48 emergency powers, and a Reichstag. Led to coalition governments.
Signed 1919: war guilt (Article 231), reparations (£6.6 billion), loss of territory and army limited to 100,000. Seen as a 'diktat'.
Spartacist uprising (1919), Kapp Putsch (1920), Munich Putsch (1923) and political assassinations.
Caused by war debts, reparations and printing money after the occupation of the Ruhr; savings were wiped out.
Rentenmark, Dawes Plan (1924), Locarno (1925), League of Nations (1926) and Young Plan (1929).
Unemployment over 6 million by 1932; collapse of the Müller coalition (1930); presidential government by Brüning, Papen and Schleicher.
Nazis were the largest party in July 1932; backstairs intrigue by Papen and Hindenburg made Hitler Chancellor on 30 January 1933.
Kiel mutiny, abdication of the Kaiser (9 November) and the Ebert-Groener pact with the army.
Bauhaus architecture, expressionist film, cabaret and the 'new woman'; conservatives saw it as decadent.
French and Belgian troops occupied the Ruhr after missed reparation payments; passive resistance followed.
A conservative war hero, he was distrusted by republicans and later used Article 48 heavily.
Propaganda, promises to all classes, anti-communism and anger at Versailles and the Depression.
Nazis won 37% in July 1932 but fell to 33% in November, raising fears they had peaked.
Reichstag fire (February 1933), Enabling Act (March 1933), Gleichschaltung, trade unions banned, one-party state (July 1933).
June 1934: Röhm and SA leaders killed; secured the support of the army. Hitler became Führer when Hindenburg died (August 1934).
Schacht's New Plan, Göring's Four-Year Plan (1936) for autarky and rearmament; reduced unemployment through public works and conscription.
SS, Gestapo, concentration camps; Goebbels controlled media, rallies and culture.
Hitler Youth, League of German Maidens, Kinder, Küche, Kirche for women, Strength through Joy; relations with churches (Concordat 1933).
Boycott (1933), Nuremberg Laws (1935), Kristallnacht (1938), ghettos, Wannsee Conference (1942) and the Final Solution.
Edelweiss Pirates, White Rose, Swing Youth, the churches (Niemöller, Galen) and the July Bomb Plot (1944).
Total war from 1943 under Speer and Goebbels; rationing, bombing raids, forced labour and collapse in 1945.
Agreement with the Pope: the Catholic Church stayed out of politics in return for religious freedom.
Membership compulsory from 1936 and enforced in 1939; taught loyalty, fitness and Nazi ideology.
Teachers had to join the Nazi Teachers' League; the curriculum stressed race, PE and history.
Marriage loans, the Mother's Cross and pressure to leave work, reversed partly in wartime.
The idea of a 'people's community' united by race, excluding 'undesirables' such as Jews and Roma.
Roma, homosexuals, the disabled (T4 euthanasia programme) and 'asocials' were persecuted.
Recorded Hitler's plans for expansion, used to show his aims for war.
